subject: Comments
comment: I am Alicia Hernandez Ramirez and a member of the stop the Homelessness coalition and Involved in the Advocacy for the Homeless and the Addicts with personal lived experiences in both categories and witnessing the abuse and the exploitation of all of Us who are in vulnerable situations and others using those vulnerabilities to abuse Us and Exploit Us. that I am now engaged everyday speaking to the Homeless and listening to their stories upon stories of the way they have been treated since the Operation Rio Grande came into effect and closing down the main shelter and causing many homeless individuals to find shelter in other areas thru out the valley and I really don't like to use the term Homeless any more since speaking to a man who I recently met and interviewed who goes by the street name "Trigger" and that day I asked him in our interview what are some of the changes he would like to see come forth in the Housing Plan that would benefit all on these streets as a whole and not just a selected few? And the first thing he asked is that Government Officials stop using the word Homeless when referring to all of Us living on these streets, and the reason he said that was because he said it is a form of discrimination to label us like that only because now they want to categorize Us because our home is different than the rest of societies and his discription of a home is wherever you make it whether its inside of a tent which also has for walls or anywhere else a home is a home no matter where you are because it is where your heart is' and in talking to him and several others and their own personal stories and seeing them while speaking to me with tears from their eyes sharing traumatic stories of the abatements and their camps getting bulldozed and losing personal and important documents and items, devices, bedding and basically everything they owned that they haven't really healed from those traumatic experiences and so with that being said I want to personally share this information with you to please share this information to anyone in salt lake city who is Homeless or has experienced Homelessness so they have a chance to share their trauma induced stories with others experiencing the same thing so they know and feel that they are not alone in this road to healing and recovery and taking this step into Trauma Awareness will be such a big help on their personal journeys. We are not our addictions or our circumstances, Or our Traumas that made us this way, or the way we chose to cope with our traumas. We are all still human and should not be categorized or excluded or discriminated or even made to feel like we do not belong or even worse alone. We have the same rights as anyone else in this City to be treated with dignity and respect and the same Justice f or All. Please Share

subject: Re: How to protect Capitol Hill in upcoming July 24th celebration was the Sandhurt fire burns
comment: As you are aware, the neighborhood association up here on Capitol Hill brings together neighbors to help with 'monitoring' on the two big firework holidays, 4th and 24th. We 'man' intersections to educate the public on the hazards of fire up these canyons. We NEVER limit access to the trails, but instead, provide education on responsible behavior while enjoying the views from Ensign Peak and other outlooks from the top of Capitol Hill. It is always a challenge dealing with the city explaining that we are NOT limiting access or infringing on individuals' rights. Now that the Sandhurst fire continues to burn and 40 houses are evacuated for safety, I am very concerned about your plan to help limit access to the fire areas and also viewpoint areas, given the gravity and size of the current fire. You are likely aware of the resources it is taking to fight this fire—helicopters, firefighters from many surrounding fire districts, at least one plane dropping retardant. I live on East Capitol. I witnessed the helicopters right below my back yard, dipping into City Creek to load buckets of water to fight the fire. They only stopped when it became dark. Fighting the fire in these part of the city is not as simple as hooking up to a hydrant. What happens if on July 24th, someone decides it is fun to set off fireworks or throw a lit cigarette and the grasses again ignite? Does not the safety of the multitudes of city residents and homes trump access to a recently burned out area from a very large fire? We need your support in ensuring the safety of our neighborhood and hope you will talk to whichever city leaders or organizations make sound and education decisions on this matter. Thanking you in advance for a reply to this email.................... Sidney Kaser.

I'm a pianist and have enjoyed the experience of watching performances from professionals that we would otherwise not get to see. subject: Lets talk plastic
comment: Dear All Puy, I hope this letter finds you well. I want to start by expressing my appreciation for the hard work and dedication you put into serving our community. Your efforts do not go unnoticed, and I am grateful for your commitment to making Salt Lake City a better place for all of us. Now, let's talk trash—literally. I am writing to urge you to consider implementing a ban on single-use plastic bags in Salt Lake City. I know, I know, we've all heard the same song and dance about how banning these pesky plastic nuisances might hurt businesses, but bear with me. I believe there's a sensible, phased approach that can work for everyone. Phase 1: Education and Incentives Let's start by rolling out a citywide campaign to educate residents and businesses about the environmental impact of single-use plastics. Offer incentives for businesses to switch to more sustainable alternatives, like compostable bags or encouraging customers to bring their own reusable bags. Maybe a little friendly competition between neighborhoods with prizes for the most reduced plastic use? Who doesn't love a good contest? Phase 2: Partial Ban After a year of education and incentives, we could introduce a partial ban. Focus on the major culprits first—grocery stores, big-box retailers, and chain stores. Give them a six-month grace period to transition, and provide support for small businesses to help them make the switch. Phase 3: Full Ban Once the community has adjusted to the changes, we can implement a full ban on single-use plastic bags citywide. This phased approach will allow businesses and residents to adapt gradually, mitigating any potential negative impacts. Believe it or not, some surprising places have already seen great success with similar bans. Rwanda, yes, Rwanda, has had a nationwide ban on plastic bags since 2008, and it's cleaner than ever. Closer to home, cities like San Francisco and Austin have seen significant reductions in plastic waste since implementing their bans. Even Laredo, Texas—a place you might not expect to be a green pioneer—banned single-use plastic bags back in 2015. Unfortunately the Texas courts overruled the Austin and Laredo bans but they are still cases of note. My understanding is that this should not be a problem in Utah as PC has some version of a bag ban. Beyond the environmental impact, I view the single-use plastics issue as an equity issue. All of the city's rainwater flows down to the Jordan River, which runs through District 2. As a result, we disproportionately have to deal with everyone else's litteral garbage. I spend at least one morning a week pulling plastic bags and trash out of my parkstrip because of the sheer amount of litter. It's not just unsightly; it's unfair. Our community deserves better. I know the idea of a plastic bag ban might seem daunting, but think of the upsides. Fewer plastic bags fluttering in the breeze like ghostly jellyfish, less trash clogging our waterways, and a cleaner, more beautiful city for everyone. Plus, it might save me from becoming the neighborhood's unofficial trash collector! Thank you for considering this proposal. I genuinely appreciate your hard work and dedication to our community, and I believe that together, we can make Salt Lake City a leader in sustainability and equity. Warm regards, Erik P.S. If you need help getting plastic bags out of the parkstrip, you know where to find me. I'm getting pretty good at it!
